full_judgment:
SK Sinha J : Petitioners are the opposite parties No. 1 and 3 in an arbitration proceeding under section 8(2) read with sections 11 and 12 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, who being aggrieved by the order dated 27th October, 2004 of the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1998 obtained this Rule. 

 4. It is alleged that since the petitioners denied to go for arbitration in accordance with law despite repeated requests, the contractor was constrained to file a petition to "revoke the authority conferred upon the Arbitrator who has become functus officio and, as such, dispel the cloud in the matter remove the said Arbitrator Mr Nurul Islam, Executive Engineer, LGED and appoint a new Arbitrator to act solely under section 8(2)". It is alleged that the Arbitrator misconducted himself and failed to use all reasonable dispatch in entering on and proceeding with reference and making the award and in fact, the award has lost its validity in the eye of law; as such, Mr Nurul Islam is liable to be removed. 

 5. Petitioners along with 2 others contested the case by filing a joint written objection. Their case, in short, is that the disputed work was divided into two groups, namely A and B; each having 3 items of work Nos. 1, 2 and 3. The schedule of rates of each work for item No.1 of group A was Taka 22 per cum and the total quantity of the work was 19 lac cum and the cost involved in the said work was Taka 4,18,000. The schedule of rates of earth work for item No. 2 of group Awas Taka 88 and the total quantity of the work was 33 lac cum involving a cost of Taka 29,00,400 and the schedule of rates of item No. 3 was Taka 3 per square metre having a total quantity of 19,50,000 square metre involving cost of Taka 49,500. The works of items No. 1, 2 and 3 of group B were similar to group A having the same rate per unit differing only in respect of quantities and total cost, such as for item No. 1 the total quantity was 11,000 cum involving a cost of Taka 2,52,000; for item No.3 the total quantity was 22 square metre involving a cost of Taka 66,000. The total cost as per schedule of 3 items for both the groups was Taka 66,71,500. 

 6. On getting the work order the contractor through its agent started execution of the work of item No. 1 of both the groups but it never attempted to execute the work of item No.2. The contractor was thereupon paid an advance of lump sum Taka 10,00,000 for the progress of the work. The contractor excavated the ponds and canals in excess of the required depth violating the design and thus collected extra earth for dikes. The contractor through its agent started submitting fake and fictitious bills against item No. 2 of both the groups without executing any work. As the difference of opinion between the parties over the quality and quantity of works and submission of fictitious bills cropped up; the matter was ultimately referred to sole Arbitrator Mr Nurul Islam for arbitration. The contractor submitted to the jurisdiction of the arbitration proceedings and put its claim before the sole Arbitrator. Petitioners .also submitted their written statement refuting the illegal and unjustified claims of the contractor over item No. 2. The Contractor claimed over Taka 4 crore before the Arbitrator but the Arbitrator on perusal of the connected documents and after giving a detailed hearing to the parties delivered his award on 18th May, 1995. The Arbitrator observed in the report that the contractor did not execute any work of item No.2 of any group and despite that he sanctioned Taka 22,58,883 for the works of item No.1 and for some other additional works and directed the contractor to complete the remaining works by December, 1994. The contractor didnot execute the remaining works and thereafter the petitioners had to execute the works through another contractor with huge loss. The con- tractor thereupon instituted Money Suit No. 2 of 1996 for recovery of Taka 9,75,85,555 by making false and frivolous claims, inasmuch as, as per contract the total estimated cost of works of both the items was Taka 66,71,500. The plaint was subsequently rejected by this Court in Civil Revision No. 27 of 1998 by judgment and order dated 16th July, ) 990. In the premises, the Miscellaneous Case is barred by limitation and the Court has no jurisdiction to dispose of the case. 

 8. It is contended on behalf of the petitioners that in the facts of the given case neither section 8(2) nor sections 11 and 12 of the Arbitration Act 1940 is applicable in the matter and therefore, the learned Joint District Judge has committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in allowing Miscellaneous Case and appointing an Arbitrator to arbitrate the matter. It is further contended that there is no scope for appointment of a new Arbitrator to arbitrate the matter under any provisions of the Arbitration Act, 1940 without canceling and/or setting aside the arbitration award in accordance with section 30 or 33 of the said Act and thus the learned Joint District Judge acted illegally in entertaining the petition of the contractor and appointing an Arbitrator to resolve the dispute which has already been disposed of. The learned Advocate further argues that since the contractor has submitted to the jurisdiction of the sole Arbitrator it cannot now challenge the arbitration award on the grounds that the arbitration award is a nullity as the Arbitrator was an unqualified person to arbitrate the matter. Finally, the learned Advocate argues that the learned Joint District Judge has not applied his judicial mind in making the impugned order, inasmuch as he has not assigned any reason in allowing the Miscellaneous Case and appointing an Arbitrator and therefore, the said order is liable to be interfered with. 

 10. In elaborating his submission, Mr Ariff has placed chapters II and V of the Act and submits that an arbitration agreement stands on the same footing as any other agreement; it is binding upon the parties unless it is tainted with fraud. According to the learned Advocate an arbitration is the settlement of a dispute by the decision not of a regular and ordinary Court but of one or more persons who are called Arbitrators. An Arbitrator being a tribunal chosen by the consent of the parties and unless the law allows them to chose such a Tribunal in respect of certain class of cases, they have no power to do so. Any person in whom the parties may have confidence and to whose decision they may choose to refer their disputes may be selected to act as Arbitrator, provided he is not prohibited from so acting. An award passed by a person who had no authority to make it is not an award and no decree in terms of it can be passed. 

 13. In this case admittedly the Arbitrator served a copy of the arbitration award to the contractor on 8th June, 1994 but it did not file any application in Court for a direction upon the Arbitrator to file award in Court for enabling it to file a proper application for setting aside the award under section 30 of the Arbitration Act. It has been held in the case of Md Shaft vs Md Sabir PLD 1960 (WP) Lahore 591 that if a party to the arbitration agreement does not make a request to the Arbitrator or umpire for filing award in court it can directly come to the Court and request for an order directing the Arbitrator or the umpire to file the award or a signed copy thereof in Court; such an application will be governed by Article 178 of the Limitation Act if notice of the award has been given to the applicant as provided by sub-section (1) of section 14 of the Arbitration Act. The right to apply accrues to a party immediately when an award is made. In that reported case, the relevant portion of the observations is as follows: "in my opinion, where a notice is given, or not, an application by a party to the court to direct the Arbitrator or the umpire to file the award will be covered by sub-section (2) of section 14". Similar views have been expressed in Jagadish Mohaton vs Sundary Mohatan AIR 1949 Pat 393. In that case it has been observed: 

 15. Mr Ariffhas failed to cite any authority on this point. We are unable to accept the contention of Mr Ariff for, the contractor having the knowledge about the arbitral award, it is obligatory on its part to make proper application in Court within the period of limitation. Section 14 applies in all cases whether the arbitral award has been filed in favour of the applicant or against him. After the award has been filed in Court, then the applicant will take appropriate steps either for passing a judgment in terms of the award or for remitting the award for re-consideration or to set aside award under section 17 of the Arbitration Act on the grounds mentioned in section 30. If the award is filed in Court; any party to the arbitration agreement has not filed any application for setting aside award, the Court shall after the time for making an application to set aside award has expired, or such application having been made, after refusing it, proceed to pronounce judgment according to award. An application to set aside award must be made within 30 days of service of notice for filing the award. 

 16. Section 30 deals with the grounds on which an award can be set aside and section 33 provides the procedure to be followed in making an application either for setting aside award or for arbitration agreement. An application to set aside award cannot be made in the absence of an award being filed in Court. An award can be set aside under section 30 under any of the following grounds that (a) an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted himself or the proceeding; (b) an award has been made after the issue of an order by the Court superseding arbitration or after arbitration proceeding have become invalid under section 35; and (c) an award has been improperly procured or is otherwise invalid. 

 17. On perusal of the application filed by the contractor we find that it is a peculiar type of application. In paragraph 29 it is stated "since opposite parties (petitioners) denied to go for arbitration in accordance with law this petitioner begs to prefer this petition to revoke the authority conferred upon the Arbitrator who becomes  functus officio...... ". and in paragraph 30 it is stated "since the Arbitrator misconducted himself and failed to use all reasonable dispatch in entering on and proceeding with reference and making the award and in fact and law the award has lost its validity in the eye of law as such, the learned Arbitrator Mr Md Nurul Islam, opposite party No. 7 is liable to be removed and the authority conferred upon him is also to be revoked 

 18. Admittedly the Arbitrator arbitrated the matter and the contractor submitted to the jurisdiction of the Arbitrator and therefore, the statements in paragraph 29 were false statements, inasmuch as there was no scope for revocation of the authority of the Arbitrator who had already arbitrated the matter and fulfilled the functions reposed upon him. Thus, the question of not entering with the reference does not arise at all. Secondly, there is no allegation that the Arbitrator has left undecided some important issues raised by a party which are covered by a term of reference; the question of invalidity would not arise. If the Arbitrator has misconducted within the meaning of clause (a) to section 30, the period of limitation for setting aside an award is 30 days under Article 158 of the Limitation Act. Moreso, the contractor did not file the application under section 30 for setting aside award although it took the grounds available for setting aside award under section 30; it had filed application under section 8 read with sections 11 and 12 of the Arbitration Act. 

 19. Section 8 attracts to a case where the Court orders the filing of an arbitration agreement under section 20. Section 8(1) gives power to a Court to appoint an Arbitrator on the failure of the parties to do so; if (a) there is a valid arbitration agreement; (b) there is provision in the arbitration agreement for appointment of an Arbitrator by consent of the parties; and (c) all the parties do not concur in the appointment of Arbitrator and notice to the parties is given. Where the Arbitrator had arbitrated the dispute; sections 8 or 20 has no manner of application in such case. Where the Arbitrator refuses to act or becomes incapable of acting or when he does not make under section 8, the proper remedy of a party is to apply for his removal under section 8 or section 11. The antithesis between the two terms 'neglects or refuses' used in section 8(I )(b) show that the word neglect is meant to cover all cases other than those of positive refusal and is not confined to cases of negligence alone. If the Arbitrator fails to make the award within the time fixed, it can be said that he has neglected to do what he had undertaken and the provisions of section 8(1)(b) would in that event apply. Where an award is given the Arbitrator ceases to function and becomes incapable of action within the meaning of section 8(1)(b). If the award is set aside by the Court one party can give notice to the other party to concur in the appointment of Arbitrator and if other party fails to concur the first party can approach the Court under section 8(2) for appointment of Arbitrator. 

 21. These views have been approved in a later case in Collector of Central Excise, Baroda vs Messrs AS Enterprises (P) Ltd AIR 1990 SC 53. It has been observed that the provisions of res judicata are based on principles that there shall be no multiplicity of proceedings and there shall be finality of proceedings. This is applicable to the arbitration proceedings as well. We find no reason to depart from the views expressed by the Supreme Court of India. In view of the above, we hold that the prayer of the contractor for a second reference to arbitrate the dispute is incompetent. 

 25. Where a party to an arbitration having a clear knowledge of the circumstances on which he might have founded an objection to the Arbitrators proceedings to make their award, did submit to the arbitration going on and allowed the arbitrators to deal with the case as it stood before them, taking his chance of the decision being more or less favourable to himself it is too late for him after award has been made to insist on the objection. In Manindra Nath Mandal vs Mahananda Ray, 15 Cal Law Journal 360 it has been observed that where the defendants even after becoming aware that the name of one Arbitrator was fraudulently entered in a reference to arbitration did not protest but submitted to their enquiry; they cannot afterwards repudiate the position by alleging the inclusion of a wrong person among the Arbitrators. 

 27. Now let us consider whether in the facts of the given case, the decision referred by Mr Ariff in Messrs Concord Engineers and Construction Ltd is applicable in this case. In that case, the appellant Messrs Concord Engineer Construction Ltd got a work order for construction of some flyovers in the Dhaka City, one at Mohakhali and another at Banani and a formal contract was executed on 3rd September, 1990. After 5/6 months of the execution of the contract, the Government rescinded it and decided not to go with the construction of the flyovers. The appellant referred the matter to the Additional Chief Engineer and claimed over Taka 30 crore as Compensation. On receipt of the claim the Additional Chief Engineer asked the appellant to submit its claim in details. The appellant without complying with the request wrote to the Additional Chief Engineer requesting him to appoint an Arbitrator informing him that it had already appointed one Arbitrator on its behalf to arbitrate the dispute. The Additional Chief Engineer did not appoint any Arbitrator. After some time waiting, the appellant requested its Arbitrator to start arbitration proceeding as sole Arbitrator. The sole Arbitrator after entering into the reference served notice upon the parties and gave an award of Taka 15 crore and odd as compensation to the appellant. 

 29. Nowhere in the agreement such procedure for appointment of Arbitrator has been provided and in the premises, the respondents filed an objection under sections 16 and 31 of the Arbitration Act for remission of the award. In that case it was argued on behalf of the appellant that in view of surrendering to jurisdiction of Court challenging the award, the award was not void ab initio the High Court Division erred in law in setting aside the judgment and order of the Subordinate Judge making the award rule of the Court. The appointment of a sole Arbitrator being contrary to the clauses B 6.31 and 25 of the tender agreement, the filing of objection under sections 16 and 31 was not surrendering to the jurisdiction of the Arbitrator or divesting the authority to the Arbitrator to pass the award and since the award has been void ab initio, no question of surrendering to the jurisdiction of the Arbitrator by filing objection arose at all. While maintaining the judgment of the High Court Division the Appellate Division observed: 

 30. So we find that the said case is quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case. In that case there was clear provision for appointment of a designated Arbitrator but in violation of the provision the appellant appointed an Arbitrator of its choice. In this case neither in the arbitration agreement nor from the correspondences it could be inferred that the parties agreed that the arbitration should be referred to a Superintendent Engineer. The contractor came out with a case that the award was given by a non designated Arbitrator but it failed to substantiate its claim. The contractor had surrendered to the jurisdiction of the Arbitrator and after exhausting all remedies available and wasting for about 4-1/2 years after giving the award came up with a frivolous application for appointment of a fresh Arbitrator under section 8, which provision has no manner of application in the case. If the contractor's application be treated as one under section 30 of the Arbitration Act, it is hopelessly barred by limitation. The application cannot be treated as one under section 8, inasmuch as, the grounds on which such application can be filed are not available to the contractor. In view of the above, the application is a misconceived one. '
